open_points.subject: context
open_points.text: The service runs on Linux and on no other host, no version named
open_points.question: Which Linux kernel, user-space ABI, distribution, architecture and minimum versions are the supported execution baseline?
options: Support every Linux version on which dependencies install
Name a minimum kernel and user-space baseline
Name one deployment image and kernel combination
open_points.default_guess: Name and test the deployment image and a minimum supported kernel version.

witness.initial: Two Linux deployments use different kernel versions.
events: The deployer starts the same service build on each deployment.
The service reaches a filesystem call whose flags or error behavior differs between the kernels.
outcomes: Both deployments are supported because both hosts are Linux.
Only the deployment matching an unstated assumed baseline is supported.

open_points.subject: context
open_points.text: The service runs on Linux and on no other host
open_points.question: Does “host” mean the host kernel, the container or VM guest, or the service's user-space image?
options: Require a Linux host kernel even when the service runs in a VM or container
Require only a Linux guest or container environment
Require both the host kernel and service environment to be Linux
open_points.default_guess: Treat the kernel visible to the service as the host and require it to be Linux.

witness.initial: A Linux container runs under a non-Linux desktop through a Linux virtual machine.
events: The deployer starts the service in the container.
outcomes: The deployment is supported because the service observes a Linux kernel.
The deployment is unsupported because the physical host is not Linux.

open_points.subject: context
open_points.text: a call these rules rely on
open_points.question: Which service operations rely on each listed Linux/filesystem call, and what exact syscall or library API realizes each requirement?
options: Specify the operation-to-primitive mapping here
Let each later module choose its own primitive
Treat every filesystem operation as relying on every listed property
open_points.default_guess: Specify one operation-to-primitive mapping and the required flags and errors for each primitive.

witness.initial: Two modules must safely access the same service-managed path.
events: One implementer uses a pathname check followed by an ordinary open.
Another implementer uses a descriptor-relative open with no-follow flags.
outcomes: A link substitution between check and open can redirect the first module.
The second module rejects or avoids the substituted link.
witness.observer: The API caller and filesystem owner

open_points.subject: context
open_points.text: a Linux or file system on which a call these rules rely on — opening without following a link, opening a folder as a folder, opening without blocking, creating exclusively, locking, renaming, flushing — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported
open_points.question: Which filesystems, mount configurations and remote or overlay filesystems are supported, and who ensures they provide the required semantics when the service does not test them?
options: Name an allowlist of filesystems and mount constraints
Make deployment responsible for validating the required capabilities
Declare all Linux filesystems supported unless a failure is observed
open_points.default_guess: Make deployment responsible for selecting and validating a documented allowlist of filesystem and mount configurations.

witness.initial: One deployment stores service files on a local filesystem and another on a network-mounted filesystem with different lock or rename guarantees.
events: The deployer starts the service without a capability test.
Two callers concurrently update the same object.
outcomes: Both deployments are considered supported and must produce the same result.
The network-mounted deployment is silently outside support, although no declared check identifies it.

open_points.subject: context
open_points.question: Must opening reject only a symlink in the final path component, or also prevent symlink traversal in every ancestor component, and what error is produced?
options: Reject only a final-component symlink
Reject symlinks in every path component
Permit trusted ancestor symlinks but reject an untrusted final symlink
open_points.default_guess: Resolve relative to a trusted directory descriptor and reject symlinks in every untrusted component.

witness.initial: A requested regular file has no final-component symlink, but one ancestor directory is replaced by a symlink to another tree.
events: A caller requests the file.
The service opens the path.
outcomes: The open succeeds because only the final component is checked.
The open fails because no path component may be followed through a symlink.
witness.observer: The caller and owner of the other tree

open_points.subject: context
open_points.text: opening a folder as a folder
open_points.question: What exact directory-open guarantee is required: an atomic directory-only open, a post-open type check, or merely successful enumeration, and how are substitutions and errors handled?
options: Use an atomic directory-only open flag
Open first and verify the descriptor refers to a directory
Check the pathname before an ordinary open
open_points.default_guess: Use an atomic directory-only descriptor open and return a defined invalid-path error for non-directories.

witness.initial: A path initially names a directory and is replaced with a regular file during access.
events: A caller triggers an operation on that path.
The service attempts to open it as a folder.
outcomes: The service opens the replacement and rejects it only after inspection.
The directory-only open fails atomically without accepting the replacement.

open_points.subject: context
open_points.question: Which objects must be opened nonblocking, what maximum waiting behavior is allowed, and how are would-block or unsupported errors exposed or retried?
options: Use nonblocking mode for every filesystem open
Use it only for object types that can block, with defined would-block handling
Interpret the phrase as requiring only that request handling have a timeout
open_points.default_guess: Use nonblocking open for potentially blocking special objects and map would-block to a defined immediate error without retry.

witness.initial: An untrusted path names a FIFO with no peer.
events: A caller submits the path.
The service opens it.
outcomes: The request waits for a peer or until an unstated timeout.
The open returns immediately and the request receives an error.

open_points.subject: context
open_points.question: Which objects are created exclusively, what namespace determines exclusivity, and what result is returned when the target already exists?
options: Fail whenever the final name already exists
Create a unique temporary name and later replace the destination
Use exclusive creation only for locks, not persisted output
open_points.default_guess: Use atomic exclusive creation for newly named objects and return an explicit conflict when the name already exists.

witness.initial: No object exists at a target name.
events: Caller A and caller B concurrently request creation at the same name.
Both service workers attempt creation.
outcomes: Exactly one creation succeeds and the other receives a conflict.
Both requests proceed through separate temporary objects and one later replaces the other's result.

open_points.subject: context
open_points.question: What is locked, whether the lock is advisory or mandatory, shared or exclusive, process- or descriptor-scoped, how long acquisition may wait, and what failure or stale-lock behavior applies?
options: Use blocking exclusive advisory file locks
Use nonblocking advisory locks and return conflict
Use lock files created exclusively
Use an in-process lock only
open_points.default_guess: Use nonblocking exclusive advisory locks held by an open descriptor for the full critical section, returning a defined conflict when unavailable.

witness.initial: Two service workers can update the same persisted object.
events: Worker A acquires its chosen lock and starts an update.
Worker B attempts the same update using a different reasonable interpretation of “locking”.
outcomes: Worker B waits and later performs a serialized update.
Worker B immediately fails with a conflict or proceeds because its lock scope does not coordinate with worker A.

open_points.subject: context
open_points.question: Must rename be atomic, may it overwrite an existing destination, must source and destination share a filesystem, and what state is required after cross-device or collision errors?
options: Require same-filesystem atomic rename with replacement
Require same-filesystem no-replace rename
Fall back to copy and delete across filesystems
open_points.default_guess: Require a same-filesystem atomic rename, state explicitly whether replacement is allowed, and reject cross-filesystem moves without copy-and-delete fallback.

witness.initial: A completed temporary file is ready while a destination with the same name already exists.
events: The service commits the temporary file by rename.
outcomes: The existing destination is atomically replaced.
The rename fails and the existing destination remains unchanged.
witness.observer: The caller and any concurrent reader

open_points.subject: context
open_points.question: What must be flushed, with which operation, and what durability guarantee is required before success is returned, including whether the containing directory must be flushed after creation or rename?
options: Flush only language-level buffers
Flush file contents and metadata
Flush the file and every affected containing directory
Do not promise crash durability
open_points.default_guess: Flush file contents and metadata, then flush the affected containing directory after creation or rename before reporting success.

witness.initial: The service has written and renamed a result but the containing directory entry has not been durably flushed.
events: The service reports success to the caller.
The machine loses power immediately.
outcomes: The acknowledged result may be absent after restart because flushing meant only the file or user-space buffer.
The acknowledged result and its directory entry must survive because success required both file and directory durability.

open_points.subject: context
open_points.text: is unsupported: the service neither tests for it nor defines what it does there
open_points.question: How does deployment determine that an environment is supported when the service performs no test, and is startup rejection, undefined runtime behavior, or deployment-time prevention required?
options: Enforce the platform and filesystem constraints in the deployment route
Let operators attest to them manually
Allow startup everywhere and classify failures afterward as unsupported
open_points.default_guess: Require the deployment route to enforce a named Linux and filesystem capability baseline before the service starts.

witness.initial: A deployment uses a Linux filesystem whose rename or lock semantics do not meet the unstated assumption.
events: The deployment route installs and starts the service without testing that property.
A caller performs the affected operation.
outcomes: The deployment should have been prevented by an external support check.
The deployment is allowed, and any resulting behavior is outside the specification with no defined signal.
